# Back to the rule, applied to a real case [20 min]{.time} {#back-to-the-rule}

::: notes
**Goal.** Each doctor runs the three questions on one of their own outputs, decides use, fix or discard, and posts one Monday line.

**Have ready.** The three-question card and the module page open in tabs, to paste both links in the chat. For anyone with no output, the referral-letter prompt in the prompt library, which holds Case C. Breakout rooms of two (one of three if the count is odd). A tally on the chalkboard (press B): Q1, Q2 and Q3 for "no", then invented, omitted, altered, fabricated citation.

**Watch for.** "It looks right" as the evidence, or "I asked the tool" as the source. The Lab Three output picked again: this round is for the output that looks fine. Real patient detail: stop it and switch to a synthetic case. Tool debates in the synthesis: steer back to the three questions.

**If asked.** Every output at work? Scale to the stakes; anything that goes in a chart or leaves your hands, yes. My honest answer to question 3 is no? That is the signal to slow down, not the finding to accept: verify against the source, or leave AI out of that piece. Everything came out yes? Fine, if question 2's evidence names something you opened; a yes with no evidence is a maybe.

**Bridge.** "You have checked your own work. The last check of the day is on the whole weekend: twenty minutes, all three days."
:::

## Back to the rule {#back-to-rule}

Pick one output from Day One or Two that looks fine, not the one from Lab Three. Only outputs made from the course's synthetic cases.

[Could I defend this to a colleague?]{.pill}

[Does it point to something I can verify?]{.pill}

[Would I catch it if it were wrong?]{.pill}

No output? Run [Prompt library: referral-letter](../reference/prompt-library.qmd#p-referral-letter), then check it against [Case C](../reference/case-cards.qmd#case-c).

::: notes
**0:30.** **Say.** This is not a recap. On Day One the three questions were a card you were handed; today they are a habit you either have or do not. Pick one output from Day One or Two that looks fine, not the one you took apart in Lab Three. Only outputs from the course's synthetic cases, nothing from a real patient. Four steps: alone, a breakout pair, the group, then your Monday line.

**Do.** Paste the module page link and the three-question card link in the chat. No output? The referral-letter prompt in the library, run on Case C, makes one in two minutes; the clock does not stop.
:::

## The check card {#check-card}

| The card | What you write |
|---|---|
| 1. Could I defend this to a colleague? | Yes or no, and the evidence |
| 2. Does it point to something I can verify? | Yes or no, and the evidence |
| 3. Would I catch it if it were wrong? | Yes or no, and the evidence |
| Decision | Use, fix, or discard |
| Kind of error | Invented, omitted, altered, fabricated citation, or none found |

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 2 min]{.tag} Copy the card from the [module page](../day3/m8-back-to-the-rule.qmd#back-to-the-rule) into your notes. Mark every number, name, date, dose and source. Check against the case card, not the tool.
:::

::: notes
**2:30.** **Say.** This is the card on the module page, laid out for one output. Copy it into your notes. For each question write yes or no, and the evidence: exactly what you opened. Finding nothing wrong is a valid result; an empty evidence line is not. Check against the source, not against the tool: here the source is the case card. Then decide, and name the kind of error. Leave the Monday line for the end. A no is not a failure; it is the check working.

**Do.** Solo: start a two-minute timer and keep this slide up. Post "30 seconds left" in the chat. Answer card questions in the chat; do not judge anyone's output.
:::

## Defend it to a colleague {#defend-it}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
[You]{.t}

Share your marked output and card, on screen or in the breakout chat. Say your decision aloud. Change the card wherever they find something.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card .teal}
[Your partner]{.t}

Ask "where did that come from?" about each mark. Point at anything unmarked.
:::
:::
:::

If you disagree, the source decides: not either of you, and not another AI.

::: {.move .pair}
[Pair · 6 min]{.tag} A breakout room of two. Three minutes each, then swap.
:::

::: notes
**6:30.** **Say.** You checked alone first, so whatever your partner catches is something you really missed. Partner: ask "where did that come from?" about each mark, and point at anything unmarked. Change your card wherever they find something. If you disagree, the source decides, not either of you and not another AI. Swap at three minutes. This is the last breakout step of the weekend.

**Do.** Pair: rooms of two for 6 minutes, with reminders at 3 minutes and 1 minute left. Look in on a few rooms; if you hear "looks right" with nothing opened, ask "what did you open?" **No breakout rooms:** everyone types their decision (use, fix or discard) and the one mark they are least sure of in the chat; read three aloud while the group asks "where did that come from?"
:::

[A measure of these outputs, not of any tool.]{.teal}

:::

::: notes
**2:30.** **Say.** Three questions, one at a time. First: which question most often came out no? Type 1, 2 or 3. Second: which kind of error came up most? Type the word: invented, omitted, altered, fabricated citation, or none. Third: what would you change to catch it faster? One sentence. Whatever the group finds is a measure of these outputs, not of any tool.

**Do.** Chat: click once per question; read the counts and two or three answers. Tally on the chalkboard (press B). If the chat turns to which tool is best, steer back: which of the three questions would have caught it?
:::

## Your Monday line {#monday-line}

| Too vague | Specific enough |
|---|---|
| Be more careful with AI. | Open the source for every number and name before I use a draft. |
| Follow the rule. | Read every instruction in a patient handout against the source before I give it out. |

Each specific line names an action, a thing to check, and a moment.

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 90 sec]{.tag} Write your Monday line on your card, then post it in the chat. One sentence, starting with a verb.
:::

::: notes
**2:00.** **Say.** The first day you are back at work is the test of the whole weekend. Make your line small enough to do that day and specific enough that you would know if you had not: an action, a thing to check, a moment. Write it as the last row of your card, then post it in the chat.

**Do.** Chat: give 90 seconds, then read three aloud. If one is vague, ask what the action is, what gets checked and when. In the last 30 seconds, the bridge: "You have checked your own work. The last check of the day is on the whole weekend: twenty minutes, all three days."
:::

# Assessment quiz [20 min]{.time} {#assessment}

::: notes
**Goal.** Every doctor takes the quiz under the same, clearly stated conditions and knows where to practice afterward.

**Have ready.** Your confirmed quiz sheet: open or closed book, how it is delivered and handed in, what to do when finished. Settle every item before Day Three; the list is in the instructor guide (Open decisions, Assessment). The practice bank on the assessment page open in a tab.

**Watch for.** Improvising a policy under pressure: "let me confirm" beats a guess. Hints, and anyone reaching for an assistant by habit: state the rule before it starts. Anxiety: say once that the quiz shows what stuck, not a judgment of them as doctors.

**If asked.** Open book? May I use an AI tool? Pass mark? Will we go over the answers? Answer only from your confirmed sheet; if an item is not confirmed, say so and say when you will tell them. Does the certificate depend on the result? It is a certificate of completion for every doctor who finishes the weekend; anything beyond that comes from the sheet. Can I practice first? The practice bank is separate from the quiz and is for afterward.

**Bridge.** "Quiz done. Ten minutes left: your certificate, four things to keep, and a plan for your first two weeks."
:::

# Certificate and closing [10 min]{.time} {#closing}

::: notes
**Goal.** Each doctor knows what the certificate is, can say the four things to keep, and has written down one low-risk task and one colleague to teach.

**Have ready.** Certificates ready, to be issued by the process on your confirmed sheet. The feedback link, ready to paste in the chat. The closing section of the module page open for the plan's wording.

**Watch for.** A CME, CPD or accreditation claim slipping in, from the group or from you. The closing crowding out the plan: cut "what this course did not cover" to one minute before you shorten the first two weeks. Tool endorsements: the course recommends none.

**If asked.** CME or CPD hours? It is a certificate of completion; the course makes no CME, CPD or accreditation claim, and the accreditation position is in the instructor guide. Which tool on Monday? Whatever your institution approves for patient information; for non-patient tasks, a general assistant you already have; availability changes, so check. Who is responsible if an AI-drafted note is wrong? A medico-legal question outside this course: "AI drafts. You decide" says where the decision sits, not a legal position; ask your data protection officer or legal team. Can I share the site? Answer from your confirmed sheet.

**Bridge.** "Take the low-risk task you just wrote down and run the check on its first output. AI drafts. You decide."
:::

**3:00.** **Say.** Four steps, in order, each small on purpose. At the start of week one, pick one low-risk task, such as rewording an email to a colleague or a first outline for a talk, and run the check on every output; keep patient data out of it. Also in week one, keep a prompt library: prompts that gave a draft you would use, with a placeholder where the facts go, never the facts. :::

[The rule is where to start. Then ask someone who works in that area.]{.pill}

::: notes
**1:30.** **Say.** Be honest and brief. This weekend was about text: drafting, summarizing and checking, with general assistants and a few purpose-built tools. Four areas were outside it. Imaging AI: tools that analyze scans, slides and other images. Clinical decision support and regulation: systems that recommend inside clinical workflows, and the rules on how they may be used. Medico-legal questions: who answers for an AI-drafted note that turns out wrong. The rule tells you where the decision sits; it is not a legal position, so ask your data protection officer or legal team. AI built into your hospital's record system, in depth. For all four, ask someone who works in that area.

**Do.** No move here; talk it through. If the clock is short, cut it to one minute.
:::
